entries.mnemonic: The lek hiding in the middle of electron is the Thai word for small — and an electron is the smallest thing anyone has ever bothered to name. A man stands in a hall of vast machinery built entirely to look at one speck. (▲ high and taut, said fast, a tiny word)
entries.headline: lék.
entries.scene: A cavernous laboratory hall filled with enormous copper coils and pipework. A physicist in a white coat stands dwarfed at the centre, bending to peer at a single minuscule point of blue light suspended between two great metal plates.

entries.mnemonic: The chow bell goes at the end of harvest and the whole village comes: grandmothers, farmhands, babies on hips, every last one of them holding a bowl. ชาว is not a crowd, it is the folk of a place, the people of somewhere, and chow brings all of them out at once. (— flat and level, one long even call)
entries.headline: chaao!
entries.scene: A village clearing at dusk with a long trestle of steaming pots. A hundred villagers of every age converge on it from the fields and houses, bowls in hand, some running, an old woman carried between two grandsons.

entries.mnemonic: Mark my— and he never finishes the sentence, because the crowd coming through the gate is past counting. mâak-maai is more than anyone can mark: many, plenty, loads of the stuff. (↓ falls hard on mâak, then maai levels out flat)
entries.headline: Mâak-maai!
entries.scene: A man stands on a wooden crate at the edge of a temple fairground, arm half raised and mouth open mid-sentence, overwhelmed as an enormous crowd streams past him in every direction and fills the frame to the horizon.

entries.mnemonic: Say RUCKSACK and drop the last k: rák-sǎa. His is twenty years old, a quilt of mismatched patches, every strap restitched a dozen times, and he is sewing another patch on now rather than buying a new one. That keeping-a-thing-going is the word. (↑ the second half climbs, the lift of the pack going back on)
entries.headline: rák-sǎa.
entries.scene: An old hiker sits on a boulder sewing a fresh patch onto a battered canvas rucksack across his knees, needle raised mid-stitch. The pack is a quilt of mismatched patches. Mountain trail, cold clear morning.

entries.mnemonic: The fairground strongman brings the mallet down and the puck goes all the way up the tower: the bell at the top rang, and rang loud enough to stop the music. แรง is that. Force, power, the strength that made the bell speak. (— flat and level, held like a struck note)
entries.headline: …and it RANG.
entries.scene: A night fairground high striker. A heavily built man in a vest has just swung a mallet onto the pad, the puck streaking up the tower, and the brass bell at the top is jolting sideways mid-strike.

entries.mnemonic: The whole village turns out for the harvest supper: every family at one long table down the middle of the barn, bowls going hand to hand over the heads of the children. Chow, in a barn. That crowd — not the town, not the government, the people of the place — is chaao-bâan. (↓ falling, the weight of the word comes down on bâan)
entries.headline: chaao-bâan.
entries.scene: Forty villagers of every age crowd both sides of one long trestle table, passing bowls of food hand to hand. Children under the table, a dog, hay bales to the rafters. Barn interior, lantern light, blue dusk.

entries.mnemonic: Say the first syllable of kayak and stop there: kǎai. A river trader has eight of them roped nose to tail along the bank and is holding a ninth over his head, shouting across the water at the tourists. Whatever he has, he sells it. (↑ rising, the voice climbs like the arms)
entries.headline: kǎai!
entries.scene: A muddy riverbank lined with brightly painted kayaks roped nose to tail. A wiry trader in shorts stands on an upturned hull holding one small kayak above his head with both arms, shouting across the water toward a group of tourists on the far bank. Hot bright midday, brown river.

entries.mnemonic: Climbing out of the taxi you count coins into the driver's palm: the kʰâa, what the ride costs. It is the same khaa that ends raa-khaa, price — said on its own now, with the voice dropping as each coin goes down. (↓ falling, the drop of money leaving your hand)
entries.headline: khâa.
entries.scene: A night street, a taxi stopped at the kerb with its rear door open. A passenger leans to the driver's window counting coins one by one into his open palm, dashboard glow on both their faces, wet tarmac reflecting neon behind them.

entries.mnemonic: A great ape with heavy jowls sits on the summit of a heap of crates and bicycles, one fist thumping his chest and one arm spread over the lot of it. Every last item is his. Run JOWL into KONG and you have jâo-kǎwng: the one it all belongs to. (↑ the second half climbs, the pitch of a claim being staked)
entries.headline: jâo-kǎwng!
entries.scene: An enormous gorilla with heavy jowls sits atop a mountain of crates, bicycles and furniture, one fist mid-thump against his chest, the other arm flung wide over the heap. Warehouse, dusty shafts from high windows.

entries.mnemonic: Mum points, arm dead straight, at the place where the two walls meet, and the boy goes and stands in it. That exact meeting of two walls is the mum: the corner, the angle. Nobody argues with the arm. (— flat and level, no rise, no give)
entries.headline: mum.
entries.scene: A plain sitting room. A woman stands with her arm extended rigidly toward the corner where two walls meet; a small boy trudges toward it with his head down and one sock falling. Afternoon light through net curtains, an armchair pushed aside.

entries.mnemonic: The stylist keeps adding rollers to the perm — one more, one more, pʰɤ̂ɤm — until the head is twice the size it started. pʰɤ̂ɤm is to add on top of what is already there: more curls, more chilli, more money. (↓ falling and firm, another roller clamped on)
entries.headline: pʰɤ̂ɤm!
entries.scene: A salon chair under warm bulb-framed mirrors. A woman's head is piled absurdly high with dozens of coloured curlers, and the stylist leans in with yet another one held ready in her fingers, both of them laughing at the size of it.

entries.mnemonic: He ducks under the table after a dropped coin and comes up short — his tie is pinned beneath the table leg and his neck will go no further. Under the table is where the tie is, and where he now lives. tâi. (↓ falling, the word drops with him)
entries.headline: tâi.
entries.scene: A man in a suit on hands and knees half beneath a dining table, neck yanked sideways because his necktie is trapped under a table leg, a dropped coin just past his fingertips. Low view, warm light.

entries.mnemonic: Two doves on a wire, turned toward each other, cooing — khûu, khûu — and the rest of the wire completely empty. A khûu is a pair: never one, always two, and they only make that sound together. (↓ falling, the drop at the end of a dove's call)
entries.headline: khûu…
entries.scene: Two white doves perched side by side on a telephone wire against a pale dawn sky, heads turned toward one another, throats puffed out mid-call. The wire runs away empty in both directions. Soft cold light, a rooftop far below.

entries.mnemonic: A monk steps off the kerb into six lanes of traffic and walks straight across without once hurrying, robes barely stirring, and the whole road stops for him. Calm is how he crosses, and CALM the British way, with the l silent, is how the word sounds. (↓ falling, steady and unhurried)
entries.headline: kâam.
entries.scene: A saffron-robed monk walks unhurried across a wide city road, hands folded, robes stirring in the wash of halted traffic. Cars and motorbikes stopped in both directions, drivers leaning out. Heat shimmer, hard sun.

entries.mnemonic: Sue stands in the middle of the room and the room comes to her: the rug rucking up, the chairs walking on their legs, an orange rolling across the boards. Everything goes to Sue. sùu is that word and nothing more. To, towards, into. (▁ low and flat, a short word that only points)
entries.headline: …sùu Sue.
entries.scene: A living room where the furniture is sliding across the floorboards toward a woman standing calmly in the centre, arms at her sides. A rug rucks up at her feet, two chairs tilt toward her mid-slide, an orange rolls across the boards.

entries.mnemonic: Prom night: the doors swing open and the whole class steps out in one movement, dressed and ready. pʰrɔ́ɔm is both halves of that — ready, and all at the same moment. (▲ high and taut, the held beat before everyone moves)
entries.headline: Pʰrɔ́ɔm!
entries.scene: The double doors of a school hall flung open at night, warm light spilling out behind a line of teenagers in formal dress stepping down onto the steps in perfect unison, mid-stride, chins up.

entries.mnemonic: This one is built, not borrowed. rúu on its own is to know. Stretch it into rúu-sùek and the knowing leaves the head and drops into the body: a woman stops in a doorway with her hand flat on her chest, knowing a thing before she has any words for it. Knowing, felt. (▁ the second syllable falls low and short, a knock under the ribs)
entries.headline: rúu-sùek.
entries.scene: A woman stands motionless in a kitchen doorway, one hand pressed flat over her heart, eyes lowered, caught in the instant of registering something. A phone lies face down on the counter behind her. Late afternoon light.

entries.mnemonic: The doctor asks which one is hurting and he smacks his own knee twice, hard: nîi. This one. Not that one, not the one from last year, this knee, the one he can reach and hit. นี่ always points at whatever is nearest to hand. (↓ falling, the voice drops with the hand)
entries.headline: Nîi.
entries.scene: A clinic examination room. A man sitting on the couch with both trouser legs rolled up slaps his own left knee with a flat palm, caught mid-strike, jaw set. The doctor leans in with a small torch, eyebrows up.

entries.mnemonic: She asked for one carrot. The grocer hands over a pack so enormous she has to hug it with both arms, greens bursting out of the top and over her face, the single carrot still held up in her fingers. A whole pack of phàk. (▁ low and clipped, stopped dead by the k)
entries.headline: phàk!
entries.scene: A small woman staggers backwards under an enormous wrapped pack of vegetables held in both arms, leafy greens bursting over her face, one carrot pinched in her fingers. The grocer grins behind his stall. Bright morning market.

entries.mnemonic: On the museum shelf the heart comes first and the lung in the jar comes after it, always after, never before. Lung, jar: lǎng-jàak. Hear the lid click shut on the end of jàak, and remember that หลัง on its own means behind. (↑ lǎng climbs, then jàak drops low and clipped)
entries.headline: lǎng-jàak.
entries.scene: A dim museum shelf of specimen jars. A curator's gloved hand rests on the second jar, which holds a pale lung suspended in fluid; the first jar beside it holds a heart.

entries.mnemonic: Yin is the female half of the old pair. Finish it the way English finishes sing and you have jǐŋ, the word for female. A dancer turns slowly out of the light and into the dark, half bright and half shadow, all in one movement. (↑ rising, the voice climbs with the turn)
entries.headline: jǐŋ.
entries.scene: A dark stage. A Thai dancer in a gold headdress and long silk skirt turns slowly mid-movement, her curved fingers and the sweep of her skirt tracing a circle; one half of her lit warm, the other lost in shadow.

entries.mnemonic: The head teacher refuses to announce it to the room. She goes along the row and tells one child, then the next, then the next — tell a, tell a, tell a — until every single one of them has had it from her own mouth. tɛ̀ɛ-lá: each, taken one at a time. (▲ the second syllable snaps up high and stops dead)
entries.headline: tɛ̀ɛ-lá.
entries.scene: A head teacher crouches beside one seated child with a hand cupped to the child's ear, mid-whisper, while the rest of the long row lean forward waiting their turn. School hall, tall windows, dust in the light.

entries.mnemonic: He has turned the kitchen out looking for his tea: cupboard doors hanging open, tins on the floor, still no cup. Tea, where? ที่ marks the place and ไหน asks which one, so thîi-nǎi is simply which place. (↓ thîi drops, then nǎi climbs as his eyes come up)
entries.headline: Tea — thîi-nǎi?
entries.scene: A small kitchen turned upside down: every cupboard door hanging open, tins and jars crowding the worktop and the floor. A man stands in the middle of it with both palms turned up and his shoulders raised, staring at an empty shelf.

entries.mnemonic: The sweep climbs down off the last chimney on the terrace, black with soot, and pulls his crooked tie straight. Soot and tie: sùt-tʰáai, the final one, the end of the row with nothing after it. (▲ tʰáai lifts high, the voice rising on the last of them)
entries.headline: sùt-tʰáai.
entries.scene: Dusk on a long terrace rooftop. A soot-blackened chimney sweep stands on the very last chimney pot of a row that recedes into the distance, straightening his crooked tie, brushes slung over one shoulder. Orange sun low behind the rooftops, smoke drifting.

entries.mnemonic: Squeeze PLAYING down into one syllable — playng — and you have pleeng. A busker on the same corner with the same battered guitar has been playing the same thing for years, and by now the man and the song have grown into each other. (— level and even, held like a sustained note)
entries.headline: pleeng.
entries.scene: A street busker with a battered acoustic guitar stands head tipped back, eyes shut mid-song, one foot tapping beside an open instrument case. A half-circle of passers-by has stopped. Evening city light, wet pavement.

entries.mnemonic: The great ape is still up on the tower, decades on, still young, still refusing to come down. Young Kong: jaŋ-kʰoŋ is still — not motionless, but unstopped, carrying on exactly as it was. (— both syllables flat and level, nothing has changed)
entries.headline: jaŋ-kʰoŋ.
entries.scene: A giant gorilla clinging to the spire of a skyscraper at dawn, one arm hooked round the mast, chest heaving, mist and rooftops far below. Pigeons wheel round him and one sits on his shoulder, entirely at home. Cold pink light.

entries.mnemonic: Put an R in front of ORB: rɔ̂ɔp. In the lighthouse the great glass orb turns all night on its bearing, flinging the same beam over the same black water, round after round after round, and it will still be doing it at dawn. (↓ falling, the beam drops away as it swings past)
entries.headline: rɔ̂ɔp.
entries.scene: An enormous glowing glass lens assembly turns on its bearing in a lighthouse lamp room, flinging one broad beam across black sea and rocks far below. A keeper stands small beside it. Night blue, hot amber light.

entries.thai: ความรู้สึก
entries.mnemonic: A qualm is a feeling that will not sit still, and kʰwaam is how the Thai starts. kʰwaam- is the noun-maker: stick it on rúu-sɯ̀k, to sense, and you get the sensing itself — the feeling. Qualm first, every time. (▁ the last syllable sinks low, the way a qualm settles in the stomach)
entries.headline: kʰwaam-rúu-sɯ̀k.
entries.scene: A man alone at a kitchen table late at night, one hand pressed flat against his stomach, brow furrowed, staring past an untouched bowl of rice. A single bulb on a cord swings very slightly above him, shadows tilting across the wall.

entries.mnemonic: A ship's hawser, thick as a man's arm, has frayed at the tip, and every ply of it springs loose in the sailor's hands like the bristles of a brush. The plaai is the far end — the point where a thing runs out and stops. (— flat and level, the rope running out)
entries.headline: plaai.
entries.scene: A sailor's weathered hands hold the frayed tip of a thick ship's rope, its strands sprung loose in every direction like a brush. Behind, the rope runs taut across a wet deck. Grey sea light, salt spray.

entries.mnemonic: A cat stretched the full length of a garden wall lets out a yowl that will not end, one flat note going on and on over the rooftops. Drop the L and there it is: yaao, long. The cat is long and the note is longer. (— dead level; the pitch never moves, it just keeps going)
entries.headline: yaaaao…
entries.scene: A long ginger cat stretched out at full length along the top of a garden wall at night, head back, mouth open in a howl.

entries.mnemonic: Knock the O off TANGO and you have tɛ̀ng. Nobody dances a tango in their work clothes: the word is getting dressed, arranged, put together properly. The same verb composes a song — cloth or music, it is all arranging. (▁ low and flat, the pause before the music starts)
entries.headline: tɛ̀ng.
entries.scene: A dressing room doorway. A woman in a fitted scarlet dance dress stands with arms raised while an older dresser kneels to pin her hem; beside her a man in a black suit adjusts his cuffs.

entries.mnemonic: The child on the trolley is terrified, so the anaesthetist leans down and sings to her — quietly, badly — right up to the moment she goes under. She sang, then the op, and between the two of them everything went completely still. Say SANG OP and let the ng slide across. (▁ low and flat, the voice settling to nothing)
entries.headline: sà-ngòp.
entries.scene: An anaesthetist in scrubs bends over a child on a trolley, one hand holding hers, mouth open in quiet song. The child's eyes are half closed, her other hand limp. Hospital corridor, theatre doors spilling white light.

entries.mnemonic: A small son stands at the chai stall with his mouth open, following the long ribbon of tea as the vendor pours it from a pot held high into one held low. He has forgotten his own cup entirely. Son, chai: sǒn-jai is exactly that, your attention gone somewhere else. (↑ sǒn climbs, then jai lands flat where his eyes are)
entries.headline: sǒn-jai.
entries.scene: A street chai stall at dusk. A vendor pours a long ribbon of milky tea from a pot held high into another held low, steam curling off it.

entries.mnemonic: Every morning at the same hour he packs a tea into the same dented flask and takes the same seat on the same bus. pà-kà-tì — pack a tea — is the way things normally are: ordinary, usual, nothing out of place. (▁ low and flat throughout, nothing remarkable happens)
entries.headline: pà-kà-tì.
entries.scene: A small kitchen at dawn. A middle-aged man in a work shirt spoons tea into a dented steel flask; his lunch tin, coat and keys are laid out on the table in exactly their usual places.

entries.mnemonic: Put a D on the front of EARN, said the British way with no r in it: dəən. He walks the four miles to the yard every morning because the bus fare would come out of what he earns. Every step is walked and every step is earned. (— flat and level, the rhythm of a long walk)
entries.headline: dəən.
entries.scene: A man in work clothes walks a long empty country road at dawn, lunch tin swinging from one hand, breath showing in the cold. A distant industrial yard on the horizon. Frost, low pink sun, long shadow.

entries.mnemonic: The gallery is silent. The artist's arm juts out, the brush touches the huge white canvas once, and that is the whole painting: one black dot in the middle of all that space. jùt is the dot. A jab, and stop. (▁ low and clipped, over as soon as it starts)
entries.headline: jùt.
entries.scene: A white gallery wall holding one enormous blank canvas with a single small black dot at its centre. The artist stands close, arm still thrust forward, a fine brush in hand, the paint still wet.

entries.mnemonic: She walks the line of her class the way a captain walks the deck in front of a crew — khruu, crew, the one who keeps the whole lot upright and moving in the same direction. One flat syllable, said with respect. (— flat and level, unhurried)
entries.headline: Khruu.
entries.scene: A sunlit Thai schoolyard. A teacher in a neat uniform walks slowly along a line of pupils standing to attention, hands clasped behind her back, inspecting them; the children stand straight-backed, one sneaking a grin. Dusty ground, green trees, hard morning light.

entries.mnemonic: Put an S in front of OAT and stop there: sòot. One man, one bowl of oats, one spoon, at a table laid for one, with five chairs still tucked in. Nobody to cook for and nobody cooking for him. (▁ low and flat, as small as the bowl)
entries.headline: sòot.
entries.scene: A man sits alone at one end of a long kitchen table eating porridge from a single bowl, one chair pulled out and five tucked in. A single mug and spoon on the drainer. Grey morning light.

entries.thai: ยินดีที่ได้รู้จัก
entries.mnemonic: ยินดี yin-dii is gladness: the two halves of the yin symbol clicking together, and ดี dii genuinely does mean good. The tail of the phrase, rúu-jàk, is knowing someone. Glad to have come to know you, and the whole thing lasts exactly one handshake. (— yin-dii sits flat and warm, then the end drops low on jàk)
entries.headline: yin-dii…
entries.scene: Two men meeting in a hotel lobby, hands clasped in a firm handshake, both leaning in slightly, genuinely pleased. Beneath their feet the polished floor carries a large circular inlay of two interlocking black and white teardrops.

entries.thai: คุณสบายดีไหม
entries.mnemonic: Four pieces you already own: khun, you; sà-baai, comfortable; dii, good; and mǎi, the little hook that turns anything into a question. Stack them in that order and you have asked after somebody's health. Nothing new to learn here, only the order. (↑ rising, the voice lifts on mǎi right at the end)
entries.headline: …sà-baai dii mǎi?
entries.scene: Two neighbours meeting on a narrow village lane in the morning. One clasps the other's hand in both of hers and leans in, eyebrows raised, mouth open mid-question, smiling warmly; the other smiles back. Laundry strung overhead, sunlight through leaves.

entries.mnemonic: Three pieces you already own, laid end to end. chǎn is I. sà-baai is the man in the hammock waving his long lazy bye. dii is good. Say them in that order and you have answered the question honestly: I am comfortable, and that is good. (— the last word lands flat and level, no fuss in it)
entries.headline: chǎn sà-baai dii.
entries.scene: A woman in the doorway of a small house raises one hand in an easy wave to a neighbour across the lane, shoulders loose, unhurried smile. A hammock on the veranda behind her. Late afternoon sun.

entries.mnemonic: Ben swings round with a glass of rye and puts the whole thing down your front. You look at the stain, look at Ben, and wave it away: mâi-bpen-rai. My, Ben, rye. Never mind, it is nothing, it is okay. (↓ mâi drops hard, then the last two float off flat)
entries.headline: mâi-bpen-rai.
entries.scene: A crowded wooden bar. A man has just turned with a tumbler and sloshed dark spirit down the front of another man's shirt; the glass is still tipped in his hand, his face frozen in horror. The soaked man is laughing, one hand raised palm out, entirely unbothered.

entries.mnemonic: A man at the bar holds one finger up over the crowd. Say noong — but grinning, lips pulled wide rather than rounded — and you land the Thai vowel: nɯ̀ng. One finger, one beer, one short low syllable. (▁ low and short, over almost before it starts)
entries.headline: Nɯ̀ng!
entries.scene: A crowded bar counter at night. A man leans in with one index finger raised high above the heads around him, grinning broadly with his lips pulled wide; the barman is already reaching for a glass.

entries.mnemonic: Two singers, one song. Neither will start without the other and neither can carry it alone, so they stand at the same microphone with their heads turned toward each other and take the same breath. sǎwng is two, and it sounds exactly like the thing it takes both of them to make. (↑ rising, the pitch climbs as they draw breath)
entries.headline: sǎwng.
entries.scene: Two singers stand side by side at a single microphone, heads turned toward each other, mouths open on the same note, one hand each on the stand. Small stage, warm spotlight, dark hall, two long shadows.

entries.mnemonic: The choir stalls seat sixty and three choristers have turned up. They sing the psalm anyway, and the one on the end holds up three fingers to count them all in. Psalm, sǎam, three: the hymn and the number come out of the mouth the same way. (↑ rising, the voice climbs like the three fingers)
entries.headline: sǎam.
entries.scene: A vast stone church interior with rows of empty carved choir stalls. Three choristers in red robes stand together in the middle of one row, mouths open in song; the nearest holds up three fingers at chest height.

entries.mnemonic: Stand in the middle of a crossroads and you can see four ways at once. Thai calls that place a sìi-yɛ̂ɛk, a four-split, because sìi is four — and it sounds like exactly what you do standing there. (▁ low and flat, a short glance down each road)
entries.headline: Sìi.
entries.scene: Seen from above: a dusty rural crossroads at midday where two straight roads meet, each of the four arms running away to the horizon across parched fields.

entries.mnemonic: Palm up, all five fingers spread, and she slaps it into his hard enough to sting — both of them laughing, hâa! Five fingers and one laugh, and the laugh is the word. Nothing else to remember. (↓ falling, the laugh drops as the hands meet)
entries.headline: Hâa!
entries.scene: Two friends meet in a high-five, palms just touching, both heads tipped back laughing, all five fingers of each hand spread wide and clearly visible. Outdoor basketball court, chain-link fence, bright afternoon light.

entries.mnemonic: Six ham hocks hang from six hooks in the butcher's window, and he counts them off along the rail with the back of his knife. Hock, hòk: the meat and the number are the same short syllable, and both stop dead at the k. (▁ low and blunt, cut off at the end)
entries.headline: hòk.
entries.scene: A butcher's window seen from inside the shop: six cured ham hocks hanging in a row from hooks on a steel rail. A butcher in a striped apron runs the back of a knife along them, lips moving as he counts.

entries.mnemonic: Seven jets tear across the sky in one arrowhead, trailing coloured smoke. Count them off as they pass — jèt — one blunt syllable for each. Seven jets, and jèt is seven. (▁ low and flat, short and hard as a jet going over)
entries.headline: Jèt!
entries.scene: Seven fighter jets in a tight arrowhead formation streaking low across a clear blue sky, coloured smoke trails fanning out behind them. Along the bottom of the frame, a crowd of upturned silhouetted faces and raised hands.

entries.mnemonic: An octopus gets into the cricket bag and comes up with a bat in every arm — eight arms, eight bats, all swinging at once while the fielders back away. BAT gives you bpàaet, and the animal does the counting for you. (▁ low and flat, cut off short by the t)
entries.headline: bpàaet!
entries.scene: An octopus rises out of a cricket bag with a wooden bat gripped in each of its eight arms, all raised at different angles, as two fielders stumble backwards, caps falling off. Village green, sunny afternoon.

entries.mnemonic: The herd files into the milking shed and the farmer counts them through the gate. The ninth cow is always the one that stops in the doorway to think about it, and the gate comes down behind her. Nine cows: gâo. (↓ falling, the gate drops)
entries.headline: gâo.
entries.scene: A milking shed doorway at dusk. Eight cows are already inside the lit shed; the ninth stands square in the open gateway, head turned back, refusing to move. A farmer leans on the gatepost with one hand raised mid-count.

entries.mnemonic: Ten small glasses along the counter and one sip from each: by the last of them she has counted the whole row without thinking about it. sìp is ten, and ten sips is the row. (▁ low and flat, short as a single dry sip)
entries.headline: Sìp.
entries.scene: A long cellar counter lined with ten small tasting glasses. Nine stand drained; a sommelier lifts the tenth to her lips, eyes closed, her other hand spread flat on the wood. Oak barrels stacked behind her, warm lamplight.

entries.mnemonic: sìp is ten, and twenty is two tens — but not sǎwng-sìp, as you would expect. Thai keeps an older word for two in this one slot and puts it on the front: yîi-sìp. Two towers of ten coins side by side, one of them noticeably more tarnished than the other. (▁ the second half drops low and short, stopped by the p)
entries.headline: yîi-sìp.
entries.scene: Two neat towers of ten coins each standing side by side on a dark wooden counter, one tower bright and the other badly tarnished, a shopkeeper's hand resting beside them. Low warm light raking across the coins, long shadows behind.

entries.mnemonic: Sun, chart: sǎn-châat. Dawn comes up through the airport hall and the queue holds people dressed for a dozen different countries, every one of them waiting to answer the same question. Which nation are you. That answer is the sǎn-châat. (↑ sǎn climbs, then châat drops flat, like a stamp coming down)
entries.headline: sǎn-châat?
entries.scene: A glass-walled airport hall at sunrise, low orange light stretching across the floor. A long queue of travellers in varied traditional dress — embroidered coats, saris, robes, wool caps — waits at a booth where an officer leans forward with one hand outstretched, palm up.

entries.thai: ยินดีต้อนรับ
entries.mnemonic: Two halves, both honest. yin-dii is glad — the same glad you meet in pleased to meet you. dtâawn-ráp, torn and rap, is to receive. Glad to receive you is how Thai says welcome, and the door swings wide on the last syllable. (▲ ráp lifts high as the door swings wide)
entries.headline: Yin-dii dtâawn-ráp!
entries.scene: A wooden Thai house at dusk, its front door thrown wide. The owner stands in the warm light of the hallway with both arms spread and a jasmine garland over one wrist, beaming at three travellers coming up the path with bags on their shoulders.

entries.thai: ด้วยความยินดี
entries.mnemonic: It is with pleasure, word for word. dûuai is with. khwaam-yin-dii is the gladness, and dii, good, sits on the end of it. The porter sets the case down inside the door, straightens up, waves away the offered note and means every syllable. (— the last syllable lands flat and easy, no effort in it)
entries.headline: dûuai khwaam-yin-dii.
entries.scene: A hotel porter straightens up from a heavy suitcase set down inside a doorway, one hand still on the handle, the other waving away a banknote held out by the guest, smiling broadly. Bright lobby, morning light.

entries.mnemonic: It is the French word for French, slowed down and given a Thai mouth: français becomes fà-ràng-sèet. The middle of it, farang, is also the everyday Thai word for a Westerner, so France comes out as the farang country. (▁ the first two syllables sit low and short)
entries.headline: fà-ràng-sèet.
entries.scene: A pavement café under a wrought-iron balcony on a grey morning in Paris. A man in a beret plays an accordion beside a round marble table set with coffee and croissants; the great iron tower stands hazy at the end of the street. Wet cobbles, bare plane trees.

entries.mnemonic: Take ANGRY and stop it dead with a t: ang-grìt. A bowler-hatted man stands in the rain glaring at a cup of tea gone stone cold, furious and entirely silent about it. That is England. (▁ the second syllable drops low and stops short)
entries.headline: ang-grìt.
entries.scene: A grey wet street. A man in a bowler hat and long dark coat stands under a black umbrella, rain sheeting off it, glaring down at a cup and saucer balanced on a low wall in front of him, his face red with contained fury.

entries.mnemonic: Thai cannot begin a word with sp, so it slips a tiny sa in front and comes out with sa-bpeen: Spain, with a step taken in the doorway first. The heel comes down on the tiles and the guitar answers it. (— bpeen stays flat and level, like the long note held under the stamping)
entries.headline: sà-bpeen.
entries.scene: A sunlit whitewashed courtyard. A flamenco dancer in a red ruffled dress is caught mid-stamp, back arched, one arm curved high above her head; a guitarist sits behind her on a wooden chair, head bent over the strings.

entries.mnemonic: She sings one last la— down the platform and then she is gone. laa-gɔ̀ɔn: a la, and gone. It is the goodbye for someone leaving properly, not the see-you-tomorrow kind. (▁ gɔ̀ɔn drops low, the sound of a door pulled shut)
entries.headline: Laa-gɔ̀ɔn…
entries.scene: A railway platform at dusk. A woman leans out of the window of a moving carriage with one arm raised in a wave, mouth open mid-note; on the emptying platform a man watches the train shrink away.

entries.mnemonic: Say the first half of ROYAL and stop: rɔ́ɔy. The palace gate swings back and the guard comes out a hundred strong, rank behind rank behind rank, filling the whole courtyard for the sake of one man on a balcony. A hundred is the royal number. (▲ high and taut, pitched up over the drums)
entries.headline: rɔ́ɔy!
entries.scene: Rank upon rank of ceremonial guards in white and gold stand in grid formation across a palace courtyard, filling the frame to the far wall. A small figure watches from a high balcony. Dawn, pale gold light.

entries.mnemonic: The word is already yours, but English says Thai with a dip in the middle of it and the Thai word does not move at all. Hold it dead level from start to finish. ไท also means free, which is why the country reads as the land of the free. (— perfectly flat; no rise, no drop, no dip)
entries.headline: thai.
entries.scene: A wide rice paddy at dawn, the flooded fields lying mirror-flat to the horizon. A farmer in a straw hat stands upright at the edge of the water, arms loose at his sides, looking level at the far bank where a golden temple spire catches the first light.

entries.mnemonic: The old man's hand sweeps a wide arc: in my day— and he is off, describing a whole era. sà-mǎi is that era, a period, an age. The mǎi on the end climbs exactly like the mǎi that turns a sentence into a question. (↑ rising, the voice lifts as the hand sweeps)
entries.headline: …sà-mǎi.
entries.scene: An old man in a rattan chair on a wooden veranda, one hand raised and sweeping through a wide arc, eyes bright, mouth open mid-story. Four grandchildren sit cross-legged on the boards around him looking up. Late afternoon light through banana leaves.

entries.mnemonic: Three children are digging up the vegetable patch and the noise is tremendous: spades ringing on stone, shrieking, black earth going over the fence. A din. And din is the very stuff they are throwing about, the soil itself. (— flat and level, said as plainly as the ground)
entries.headline: din!
entries.scene: A back garden vegetable patch churned into a crater. Three children with spades fling dark crumbly soil over their shoulders, mouths open in shrieks, earth hanging in the air around them. A dog barks at the edge of the hole.

entries.mnemonic: A yard full of children raising a din — and a cloud of dirt with it. Every shout brings up more dust; the din and the dirt come off the same ground. din is that earth under their bare feet. (— flat and level, one steady note under the noise)
entries.headline: din.
entries.scene: A bare dusty schoolyard in hard sunlight. Half a dozen barefoot children mid-chase, mouths open shouting, a thick golden cloud of dust boiling up around their feet; their shins and hands caked with dry earth. A wall and a mango tree behind.

entries.mnemonic: Take CLOWN and drop the n: klàao. In the middle of the chaos the clown climbs onto a chair, takes his hat off, holds it over his heart and makes a short and entirely serious speech to the ring. klàao is saying as a formal act — stating a thing aloud. (▁ low and flat, the voice of someone being serious for once)
entries.headline: klàao.
entries.scene: A clown in full paint stands on a wooden chair with his hat held over his heart, mouth open mid-speech, completely solemn. Acrobats and a small elephant have stopped to listen. Circus ring, one spotlight, sawdust.

entries.mnemonic: Nothing is settled until it is tied down. The old sailor takes the rope, finds the exact spot along it and pulls a hard knot into place. Come and knot it, kam-nòt, and now the date exists. It is the word for fixing a thing to a precise point: a deadline, a price, a rule. (— flat on kam, then nòt drops low as the knot pulls tight)
entries.headline: kam-nòt.
entries.scene: Close view of a weathered sailor's hands hauling a thick rope taut and pulling a knot tight at one point along it, the rest of the rope coiling away across the deck planks.

entries.mnemonic: The old carpenter lays his hands over the boy's on the saw and pushes, pulls, pushes, until the plank is sawn through. He does not cut it for him. sǎawn is that: teaching, passing the thing on. (↑ rising, the voice climbs like the saw coming back up)
entries.headline: Sǎawn.
entries.scene: A dusty workshop. An old carpenter stands behind a boy at a sawhorse with his weathered hands laid over the boy's on the saw handle, a plank half cut through beneath them, curls of sawdust drifting in a shaft of light from a grimy window.

entries.mnemonic: Take QUALM and drop the m: kʰwǎa. At the fork she gets a qualm about it, hangs there a full second with both hands locked on the wheel — and then swings right anyway. The doubt lives in the sound; the turn is the meaning. (↑ rising, the voice lifts like the question she is asking herself)
entries.headline: kʰwǎa.
entries.scene: A car stopped at a rural fork. The driver, hands tense on the wheel, looks down the right-hand branch with a worried frown while the front wheels begin to bite that way. Lone tree, flat afternoon light.

entries.mnemonic: Same road, same hour, same jam — your regular jam, every single morning of your life. pràʔ-tɕam is the thing that happens on schedule and is always there: the regular customer, the regular route, the usual. (— tɕam levels out flat, the same every single morning)
entries.headline: pràʔ-tɕam.
entries.scene: An elevated view of a city expressway at sunrise, solid with unmoving cars stretching to the horizon between hazy office towers. A single motorcyclist threads the narrow gap between two lanes. Long shadows, exhaust haze, flat gold light.

entries.mnemonic: A rooster struts down the middle of the lane like he owns it — that guy. gài is chicken, and the cockerel is the guy who runs the yard: the dog steps round him, the hens get out of the way. (▁ low and flat, one short cluck)
entries.headline: Gài!
entries.scene: A village lane at dawn. An enormous glossy rooster struts down the centre of it, chest thrown out and tail high, while a dog and two hens step aside onto the verge. Wooden houses either side, mist between them, low golden light.

entries.mnemonic: The cockerel owns the yard. Chest out, wings flared, beak up, squaring off against a dog twice his size and winning, while the hens watch from the coop door. Some guy, says the farmer. gài is the bird, GUY is the sound. (▁ low and flat, a short blunt syllable)
entries.headline: gài.
entries.scene: A bantam cockerel stands chest out with wings flared and beak raised, squaring up to a dog twice his size that backs away with ears flat. Hens watch from a coop doorway. Dusty farmyard, golden evening light.

entries.mnemonic: A jar of jam is wedged under the door and it is the only thing holding the place open: take it away and everything shuts. เป็น bpen means to be, so jam-bpen is what has to be. Not wanted, not nice. Necessary. (— both syllables flat and level; there is nothing to argue with)
entries.headline: jam-bpen.
entries.scene: A heavy wooden door propped open by a squat jar of dark red jam jammed under its bottom edge, the door leaning its weight onto the glass. Beyond it a busy corridor of people passing through.

entries.mnemonic: kìaw is to hook — the curved blade that catches a whole armful of stalks in one pull. kàp is with. Hooked-with is how Thai says about: whatever catches on the subject comes up along with it. (▁ both syllables sit low and flat)
entries.headline: …kìaw-kàp…
entries.scene: Close on a farmer's hands in a paddy field: a curved sickle pulled through a stand of golden rice, a thick armful of stalks caught in the hook and bending with it, chaff flying up.

entries.mnemonic: Put a G in front of EARN: gəən. By the tenth of the month the little shop has already earned its whole target, and the takings have gone on past the top of the jar and out over the counter. To go beyond the mark is the word. It rhymes with dəən, walk. (— flat and level, no drama in the going past)
entries.headline: gəən.
entries.scene: A jar on a shop counter is so full of banknotes and coins that its lid will not sit down, notes spilling over the rim. The shopkeeper stands behind it, both hands raised, astonished. Warm afternoon light.

entries.mnemonic: Say the end of tyCOON, but with your lips pulled wide in a grin instead of pushed forward, and you land the Thai vowel: kʰɯɯn. The tycoon walks into the little family shop and hands back the keys and the cash box, all of it, with both hands. Returned. (— flat and level, the tone of a thing simply given back)
entries.headline: kʰɯɯn.
entries.scene: A man in an expensive overcoat holds out an open cash box and keys with both hands to an elderly couple behind a shop counter. They stare, one hand half raised. Cramped shop, cold daylight outside.

entries.mnemonic: Everything in the room is sub-par. Put a p on the end of sub-par and you have sà-pʰâap: the condition a thing is in. Good or bad, it is the state of it — a room's, a car's, a body's after a long week. (↓ pʰâap drops away, like a shoulder sagging at the sight)
entries.headline: sà-pʰâap.
entries.scene: A man stands in the doorway of a small rented room with his arms folded, unimpressed. Peeling ceiling, a stained mattress on a bare frame, a bucket catching a drip, one naked bulb.

entries.mnemonic: A whole country's work runs up one long table and into the mouth of a single vast man: farmers, bakers, dockers, all of it passed hand over hand to sate a git. SATE, A, GIT — sèet-thà-gìt, the machine that moves everything somewhere. (▁ low and clipped, the last syllable stopped dead)
entries.headline: sèet-thà-gìt.
entries.scene: Farmers, bakers and dock workers pass laden platters hand over hand up an impossibly long banquet table to an enormously fat man in evening dress being fed from silver dishes. Chandeliers, deep shadows, soot on their faces.

entries.mnemonic: The same chow as cháaw, morning — but let the voice fall instead of holding it up high and the meaning changes to rent. The morning goes up; the rent comes down, out of your hand and into the landlady's. (↓ falling, the voice drops as the notes leave your fingers)
entries.headline: Châo.
entries.scene: A shophouse doorway at dusk. A young tenant counts banknotes one by one into the open palm of an elderly landlady, who holds a ring of keys in her other hand.

entries.mnemonic: A free gift, this one: dtaai is very nearly the English word for what it means. An old man sits still in a chair by an open window and his hand falls open on the armrest, and the small bird he was holding lifts away into the light. Say die, but flat — no fall, no rise. (— level and undramatic, which is the strange part of it)
entries.headline: dtaai.
entries.scene: An old man sits motionless in a chair beside an open window, his hand fallen open on the armrest as a small bird lifts away from his fingers toward the light. Thin curtains moving, pale light.

entries.mnemonic: One tent pole juts out of line and the whole camp is chaos. The Khan rides down the row pointing with his crop — pole in, fire out, wagons straight — and in five minutes it is dealt with. Jut, then Khan: jàt-gaan, taking a mess and handling it. (— the second syllable runs out flat and long, the calm afterwards)
entries.headline: jàt-gaan.
entries.scene: A commander on horseback rides down a row of felt tents pointing with a riding crop, while people scramble to straighten ropes and stamp out a fire. One pole leans badly out of line. Grassland, dust, low sun.

entries.mnemonic: โรง is the building — the same โรง that sits in cinema, hotel and factory — and เรียน is to learn. Put the hall and the learning together and school falls out of it: roong-riian, the learning hall. Take โรง away with you; it builds half a town. (— both syllables level and even, like a held bell)
entries.headline: roong-riian.
entries.scene: A school courtyard at morning assembly. Rows of children in white shirts and navy shorts stand in the dust facing a long low building with an open verandah, hands at their sides. A teacher stands at the front with one arm raised.

entries.mnemonic: Allow me, says the old man, and he is away into a story that lasts an hour. The low sitting inside allow is lâw: to tell, to narrate, to spin the whole thing out while everyone leans in closer. (↓ falling, the voice drops as he settles into it)
entries.headline: Lâw…
entries.scene: Night. A village elder sits on a low stool beside a cooking fire, hands mid-gesture shaping something large in the air, mouth open in speech. A ring of children and adults sit close around him, faces lit orange, leaning in.

entries.mnemonic: Ma hands the child a nut and a rounded stone and guides her hands to show her how. Nothing else in that forest is doing anything of the kind. Ma, nut — má-nút, the one creature that makes a tool out of the world it finds. (▲ both syllables up high and taut, bright as the shell cracking)
entries.headline: má-nút.
entries.scene: A mother crouched on a forest floor guides her small daughter's hands, which hold a rounded stone above a hard nut set on a flat rock. Both absorbed. Dappled green light, monkeys watching from a branch above.

entries.mnemonic: Tick, and on the tock the coconut lets go. It is a hand's width above the dust now, directly over a man who has slept through the whole business. ตก is anything that falls: rain, prices, a man off a ladder. (▁ low and short, the sound of the landing)
entries.headline: tòk.
entries.scene: Beneath a coconut palm at noon. A large green coconut hangs frozen in the air a hand's width above the dusty ground, right beside a man dozing against the trunk with his hat over his face. A cat is already leaping clear.

entries.mnemonic: The knitter will not start until the wool is sorted — each kind in its own basket, thick with thick, red with red, no mixing. chá-nít is exactly that: the sort, the type, which kind of thing you are holding. (▲ both syllables high and quick, the snap of a decision)
entries.headline: chá-nít.
entries.scene: An old woman on a wooden veranda surrounded by six open baskets, each holding balls of wool of a different colour and thickness. She is placing one ball deliberately into its matching basket, knitting needles tucked under her arm. Soft afternoon light.

entries.mnemonic: On the bus the barrister balances his case across one raised knee and carries it that way the whole journey, arms folded over the top of it, letting nobody near. Carry, knee: kà-rá-nii, the case in question. (— the last syllable lands flat and is held the longest)
entries.headline: kà-rá-nii.
entries.scene: A barrister in a dark suit sits on a crowded bus with a battered leather briefcase balanced across one raised knee, arms folded over it, staring out of a rain-streaked window. Grey morning light, condensation on the glass.

entries.mnemonic: The road-mender wipes his forehead with a tarry glove and leaves a perfect black ring round one eye. Everybody who passes looks at that eye and at nothing else on him. dtaa is the eye, and the tar has drawn a circle round it. (— flat and level, an unblinking stare)
entries.headline: dtaa.
entries.scene: Close portrait of a road worker in a high-visibility vest staring straight at the viewer, one eye ringed with a smear of glossy black tar, the glove that did it still raised near his temple.

entries.mnemonic: dtaa is the eye. It is also your mother's father — the old man on the porch whose eye is on you the whole afternoon. One flat syllable, the same one you say as a casual ta, does both jobs: the watcher and the watching. (— flat and level, an unhurried old voice)
entries.headline: Dtaa.
entries.scene: Close portrait of an elderly Thai man seated on a wooden porch, deeply lined face, both hands resting on a walking stick, watching steadily with clear attentive eyes.

entries.mnemonic: A pat of butter running into a warm split bun, and a mouth halfway through the first chew. Not the bun from yesterday, not tomorrow's — this one, in your mouth, now. Pat, chew, bun: pàt-tɕù-ban, the present moment and nothing either side of it. (— the last syllable settles flat, right where you are)
entries.headline: pàt-tɕù-ban.
entries.scene: A person bites into a warm split bun, a yellow pat of butter melting and running at the edge, crumbs on their lip, eyes closed in concentration. A knife laid down on a kitchen table. Soft morning light.

entries.mnemonic: The cook sighs, then tips one more fistful of chilli into the wok anyway. sài is that: to put something in, or on — the chilli into the pot, the shirt onto your back, the sugar into the cup. (▁ low, the sound of a long breath going out)
entries.headline: sài.
entries.scene: Close on a blackened wok over a flame, a cook's hand tipping a fistful of dried red chillies into it. Steam and smoke rise into her face; her eyes are half closed and her cheeks puffed as she breathes out.

entries.mnemonic: The thing in the back yard has not moved in years: rot in the sills, rot through the floor, moss on the roof and a young tree grown straight up through the bonnet. rót is any vehicle at all, and this one is going nowhere ever again. (▲ high and taut, cut off short and hard)
entries.headline: rót.
entries.scene: A rusted-out car sits on flat tyres in a weed-choked yard, its bonnet buckled by a young tree grown up through it, moss thick on the roof, one door hanging open. Grass to the wheel arches, grey overcast.

entries.mnemonic: A phone lies face down in a puddle in the middle of the road, ringing and ringing while the rain hammers it flat, and nobody is coming for it. fǒn is that rain, and the voice climbs the way a ring tone does. (↑ rising, the pitch lifts like a phone waiting to be answered)
entries.headline: fǒn.
entries.scene: A tarmac road in a downpour, seen low and close. A mobile phone lies face down in a shallow puddle, rain bouncing off its back in bright crowns. The street beyond dissolves into grey water and blurred headlights.

entries.mnemonic: The cart sits tilted in the road with one wheel gone entirely, its axle down in the dirt and fruit spilled everywhere. kʰàat is what is wrong with it: short of something, missing a piece, not complete. (▁ low and flat, stopped short)
entries.headline: kʰàat.
entries.scene: A wooden handcart tipped at a steep angle in a dusty lane, one wheel missing altogether and its bare axle resting in the dirt, oranges spilled across the ground. An old vendor stands with hands on hips staring at the empty axle.

entries.mnemonic: Split a length of bamboo and the hollow core is cut across at intervals by hard pale rings — the joints, the places where it is divided into separate sections. Say CORE the British way with no r on the end and you have kʰɔ̂ɔ. (↓ falling, dropping onto each hard ring in turn)
entries.headline: kʰɔ̂ɔ.
entries.scene: A length of thick green bamboo lies split lengthways on a workbench, its hollow interior divided at intervals by pale hard rings, a craftsman's thumb resting on one ring. Shavings across the bench, warm workshop light.

entries.mnemonic: A rat is sitting up in the great carved chair at the head of the marble chamber, and the ministers file in and bow to it anyway. Wherever the power happens to be sitting, that is the rát: the state. (▲ high and taut, the way a title is announced)
entries.headline: rát.
entries.scene: A marble parliamentary chamber with columns and tiered benches. A large brown rat sits upright in the ornate carved chair on the raised dais, tail curled over the armrest. Two rows of officials in dark suits bow toward it, heads down.

entries.mnemonic: People press gold leaf onto the great city pillar and ask it for luck. làk is the pillar itself — and from there, anything central: the main thing, the principle that everything else is built around. (▁ low and short, solid as the stone)
entries.headline: làk.
entries.scene: A gilded stone pillar inside a shrine, heaped with marigold garlands at its base. A kneeling woman presses a square of gold leaf onto it with her thumb; incense smoke drifts across and other worshippers blur behind her in the warm dim light.

entries.mnemonic: Some red: the ribbon across the finish line. She takes it on the chest and it snaps and streams back off both shoulders, her arms already up. sǎm-rèt is that exact moment, the thing finished, the thing achieved. Clip the end of red short and the Thai is there. (↑ sǎm climbs, then rèt sits low and clipped as the ribbon breaks)
entries.headline: sǎm-rèt.
entries.scene: A runner breaking a broad red ribbon at a finish line, the ribbon torn and streaming back from her shoulders, both arms flung up, mouth open in a shout. Blurred crowd behind the barriers, other runners far back down the track.

entries.mnemonic: kʰwaam- is the noun-maker again, the qualm sound on the front; jing is true. Strike a cracked bell and it thuds — strike a true one and it rings out clean, jing. kʰwaam-jing is the truth itself, the thing that rings. (— both syllables flat and level, no argument in it)
entries.headline: kʰwaam-jing.
entries.scene: A hand swings a padded wooden mallet against a great hanging bronze bell in a temple courtyard. The bell shivers with the strike and a dozen birds burst off the eaves above it. Clear morning light, swept stone, saffron robes blurred behind.

entries.mnemonic: Hidden inside sàp-daa is the same ancient seven that sits inside September — sapta, seven, carried along by both languages since long before either met the other. A week is seven days: seven small lamps in a row along a sill, six of them lit and a hand bringing the taper to the last. (— the second syllable runs out long and flat)
entries.headline: sàp-daa.
entries.scene: A hand holding a taper lights the seventh of seven small oil lamps standing in a row along a stone windowsill, the first six already burning. Deep blue dusk beyond the window, warm pools of light on stone.

entries.mnemonic: Four men are hammering at a coconut and getting nowhere. The cook walks over, turns it in her palm and opens it with one tap of the cleaver's spine. That is the witty way: wí-thii, the method. A hard t in the middle, never an English th. (— the second syllable holds flat and long, wi-THEE)
entries.headline: wí-thii.
entries.scene: An outdoor kitchen. Four men crouch over a coconut with hammers and a rock, husk fibres scattered everywhere. Beside them a small woman in an apron holds a coconut in one palm, the spine of her cleaver tapping its middle, the shell already opening cleanly in two.

entries.mnemonic: Say the first half of CHUTNEY and stop: tɕʰút. He is two steps out of the door in the new outfit, pressed and immaculate, when the spoon tips and a gout of chutney lands down the whole front of it. The outfit was the point, and the outfit is finished. (▲ high and taut, the yelp he does not manage to swallow)
entries.headline: tɕʰút!
entries.scene: A man stands frozen in a doorway in a crisp new suit, arms held from his sides, a bright orange-brown splatter of chutney down the front of his jacket, a tipped spoon in one hand. Harsh hallway light.

entries.mnemonic: At dawn a woman kneels and spoons rice into a monk's bowl, and he will thaan it. Where kin is blunt and everyday, thaan is the soft, polite word for eat — the one you use for a guest, an elder, a monk. (— flat and level, gently said)
entries.headline: thaan.
entries.scene: Dawn on a Thai street. A woman kneels barefoot on the pavement spooning rice into the alms bowl of a monk in saffron robes, his eyes lowered and head bowed; a line of monks waits behind him in the mist.

entries.mnemonic: Someone holds a mug out to the sentry on the gate and he does not even turn his head: nah — not while he is on. NAH plus TEA gives nâa-thîi, the thing that is yours to do whether you fancy it or not, and whether the tea is going cold or not. (↓ both halves drop, firm and final)
entries.headline: Nâa-thîi.
entries.scene: A sentry stands rigid at a gatehouse in the rain, eyes fixed straight ahead, while a colleague beside him holds out a steaming enamel mug. Water runs off the peak of his cap. Wet cobbles, grey dawn light.

entries.mnemonic: Am-purr. Every cat owns a district: the wall, the three roofs and the alley it patrols twice a night, and it sits on the boundary at dusk to look the whole of it over. An amphoe is exactly that, the patch of country belonging to one office. (— both syllables flat and level, like the purr itself)
entries.headline: am-pʰəə.
entries.scene: A large cat sitting upright on a garden wall at dusk, tail curled round its feet, surveying a sprawl of tiled rooftops, alleys and treetops below. Lights are coming on in the houses. Its eyes are half closed and entirely proprietorial.

entries.mnemonic: Two pieces, and you have one of them already: dəən is the walk, thaang is the way or road. Walk plus way is how a man gets to work — the same wet pavement, the same hour, every morning of his life, in a river of other people doing exactly the same. (— both halves flat and level, the same every day)
entries.headline: dəən-thaang.
entries.scene: A man in a raincoat walks a wet city pavement in a stream of commuters all heading the same way, umbrellas overlapping, a bus pulling from the kerb beside them. Dark early morning, shopfront light on wet paving.

entries.mnemonic: เดิน is to walk, and it starts like earn with a d pushed in front of it; ทาง is the way, the road. Walk the way and you are travelling: dooen-thaang. The word is not about arriving anywhere, it is the going itself. (— both syllables flat and even, like a steady pace)
entries.headline: dooen-thaang.
entries.scene: A traveller with a heavy pack walking away from the viewer up a red dirt road that winds into green hills.

entries.mnemonic: A tour goes everywhere: every street, every corner, every last village on the map, with nothing at all left out. tʰûa is exactly that — throughout, all over, the entire lot of it, the whole country or the whole body. One word for the lot. (↓ falling, the voice sweeps down over the whole view)
entries.headline: tʰûa.
entries.scene: A traveller stands on a hilltop seen from behind with both arms spread wide, looking out over an entire valley of villages, winding roads and paddy fields that runs away in every direction to the hazy horizon.

entries.mnemonic: That boy is in the muck again. Not once, not as a treat — always, every single day, straight off the dry path and into the deepest part of it, up to the elbows. mák is the word for the thing somebody is forever doing. (▲ high and taut, cut off by the k, said through the teeth)
entries.headline: mák.
entries.scene: A small boy stands knee-deep in a brown farmyard puddle, grinning, arms spread, mud to his elbows and across his face. On the dry path a woman waits with a towel, unsurprised. Grey drizzle, farm buildings behind.

entries.mnemonic: A full tum, Ma in one chair, Da in the other, and absolutely nothing happening. No visitors, no news, the same supper as last week and the cat asleep in the same spot on the rug. tham-má-daa is a Tuesday: plain, normal, exactly as it always is. (— the last syllable runs out flat and even, the tone of nothing much)
entries.headline: tham-má-daa.
entries.scene: An older couple sit in two armchairs, one dozing with hands folded over a full stomach, the other slowly stirring a cup. A cat asleep on the rug, a cleared supper table behind. Lamp light, curtains drawn.

entries.mnemonic: At the end of the line the robot arm swings a box down and stacks it onto a wooden pallet, thump, and the pallet fills and another comes up empty behind it. pà-lìt is the making itself: what a factory does all day, every day. (▁ low and flat, the thump of the pallet taking the weight)
entries.headline: pà-lìt.
entries.scene: A factory floor at the end of an assembly line. A yellow robot arm lowers a plain sealed box onto a wooden pallet already stacked shoulder-high with identical boxes; a forklift waits to one side with its forks raised.

entries.mnemonic: The shoe has given up at the front and his big toe is straight out through the end of it. He has grown again, in a month, and the next pair will go the same way. TOE gives you toː: getting big, and the growing that does it. (— flat and level, steady as growth itself)
entries.headline: toː.
entries.scene: A child's scuffed shoe with the big toe pushed through a split across the front, the foot planted on a doorstep. Blurred behind, a parent's hands hold a pencil flat against a doorframe marked with faint height lines.

entries.mnemonic: พ่อ is PAW, the father, with a round aw in the middle. พา is PAH, with an open ah, and it means to take someone along with you. Here the pa does both: his hand closes round the child's wrist and he tows her through the crowd without breaking stride. (— flat and level, the pace never changes)
entries.headline: pʰaa.
entries.scene: A packed night market seen from behind. A tall father in a work shirt cuts through the crowd with a small girl's wrist held firmly in his hand, her feet skipping to keep up, her free hand clutching a skewer.

entries.mnemonic: jɔɔm is to give in; ráp is to receive. Give in and take it, and you have accepted. There is a rap at the door, and you can either leave it knocking or open up and receive whatever is standing out there. (▲ ráp snaps up high, the moment of taking it)
entries.headline: …ráp.
entries.scene: A man stands in his open front doorway at night, one hand still on the latch, taking a heavy wrapped parcel from a courier standing in the rain. His shoulders are dropped and his expression resigned but steady.

entries.mnemonic: This is a cousin of the English word rather than a coincidence: sà-thǎa-nii and station both come down from an old root meaning to stand. A place where things stand still a while — the train breathing at the platform, everybody waiting, nothing moving yet. (— the last syllable runs out flat and long, held like the wait)
entries.headline: sà-thǎa-nii.
entries.scene: A train stands at a platform with its doors open and heat shimmer around the wheels, a scattering of passengers waiting along the edge, one leaning out to look up the track. High roof, dusty shafts of light.

entries.mnemonic: tàt is cut and jai is heart, and the sǐn between them sounds like sin. To decide, in Thai, is to cut the sin out of your heart: end the dithering, choose the path, go. (↑ sǐn climbs in the middle, then jai lands flat and final)
entries.headline: Dtàt-sǐn-jai!
entries.scene: A woman stands at a fork in a forest path at dusk, pack already shouldered, one hand pressed flat over her heart and the other making a single decisive chopping motion in the air. Her body is turned toward the left-hand path.

entries.mnemonic: Say AROMA and stop before the last vowel: aa-rom. Bread comes out of the oven and fills the house, and the man who came in slamming doors drops his bag, shuts his eyes and softens where he stands. The smell changed the mood, and the word is the mood. (— both syllables flat and even, settling)
entries.headline: aa-rom.
entries.scene: A man in his coat stands in a kitchen doorway, bag dropped at his feet, shoulders come down, eyes half closed, facing a tray of loaves fresh from the oven. Steam rising. Warm oven light, dim hallway.

entries.mnemonic: ผู้ is the one-who, the same ผู้ that starts the words for man and woman, and ใหญ่ is big. An adult is simply the big one: the person who takes the jar off the top shelf without going up on anything. phûu-yài. (↓ phûu drops, then yài settles low, with the weight of being the big one)
entries.headline: phûu-yài.
entries.scene: A kitchen. A small girl up on tiptoe on a stool strains toward a plain jar on the highest shelf, fingers short of it by a foot.

entries.mnemonic: Knock the s off NURSE and you have the end of sà-nɤ̌ɤ. The theatre nurse holds the tray out flat, the instrument laid on it handle first, waiting for the surgeon to take it. That is what sà-nɤ̌ɤ does with an idea: puts it forward. (↑ rising, the voice lifts as the tray comes up)
entries.headline: sà-nɤ̌ɤ.
entries.scene: An operating theatre under a bright overhead lamp. A masked nurse in a green gown extends a steel tray toward a surgeon with both hands, a single clamp laid on it turned handle first. Everything beyond the lamp's circle falls into shadow.

entries.mnemonic: A crow has taken the roof of a parked car for its own: one glossy black bird planted dead centre, turning a single eye on the owner and refusing to shift for him or anybody. Say CAR the British way, with no r on the end, and you have kaa. (— flat and level, one unbothered note)
entries.headline: kaa.
entries.scene: A glossy black crow stands dead centre on the roof of a parked car, head turned to fix the viewer with one eye, wings open, while a man beside it waves an arm without effect. Morning light.

entries.mnemonic: Batting practice in the cage: he pats a ball onto the tee, squares up, bats it away, and then does the whole thing again, and again, two hundred times before the light goes. Pat, tee, bat — pà-tì-bàt, doing a thing over and over until the body owns it. (▁ low and clipped, the flat crack of the bat)
entries.headline: pà-tì-bàt.
entries.scene: A player in a helmet places a ball onto a tee with one hand, bat resting on his shoulder, a dozen balls already scattered in the netting behind him. Batting cage at dusk, floodlight glare, dust.

entries.mnemonic: A geologist lifts a long core out of the ground under an enormous moon, and everything about the place is there in its bands. kʰɔ̂ɔ is a single item, muun is the raw stuff: core and moon together, kʰɔ̂ɔ-muun, the information. (↓ falls on kʰɔ̂ɔ, then muun levels out flat)
entries.headline: kʰɔ̂ɔ-muun.
entries.scene: Night in an open field. A geologist crouches holding up a long cylindrical soil core banded in coloured layers, turning it in gloved hands under the beam of a head torch.

entries.mnemonic: gaan is the piece that turns a doing into a thing — the -ing of it. Put it in front of sùek-sǎa, to study, and you have the whole business: a room of small heads craning at a teacher holding up a jar with something growing in it, hands going up everywhere. (↑ the final syllable climbs, the lift of a question being answered)
entries.headline: gaan-sùek-sǎa.
entries.scene: A classroom of children at desks lean forward to watch a teacher hold up a glass jar with a plant growing inside it, hands raised all over the room. Late afternoon sun through tall windows, dust.
